processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted; nothing peculiar to this variety is recorded.
harvest_season: Typical of Wuyi rock teas, a single spring picking; no variety-specific timing is recorded.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips, as is usual for roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_liquor: Orange-amber, typical of a medium-roast rock tea.
appearance_wet: As with other rock teas, broad leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting notes exist; expect the roast and mineral character shared by Wuyi rock teas, and do not assume osmanthus from the name.

brewing.notes: Standard rock-tea brewing: near-boiling water and short steeps in a small vessel.

vintage_note: Sold like other Wuyi rock teas, by the year of the spring harvest and usually after the roast has rested. Check what the label means, since the name is easily mistaken for other teas.
description:
Jin Gui is a name in lists of Wuyi rock-tea varieties, and little more is on record about it. The characters mean golden osmanthus, which is what makes it confusing.

It is not Huangjin Gui, the Anxi oolong, and it is not Shui Jin Gui, one of the four famous Wuyi bushes, whose final character is different. Jin Gui is also a name for an osmanthus flower used in scenting.

Assume the usual rock-tea making, and brew it hot and quick. Its own aroma has not been described with any authority, so the name alone tells you nothing about flavour.

Before buying, confirm that the seller means a Wuyi variety, and ask for the year and growing area.
history: Little is documented about Jin Gui beyond its appearance among the varieties named in modern lists of Wuyi rock tea. Its origin and date are not established.
